props.title: Miami Connection
props.initialSlug: Taekwondo rockers battle ninja drug dealers in Miami

sections.content: **Miami Connection (1987)** (1987) stands as a glorious testament to 80s DIY filmmaking ambition colliding with martial arts mayhem. Made by Y.K. Kim, a Taekwondo instructor with zero film experience, this fever dream follows a synth-rock band called Dragon Sound who battle cocaine-dealing ninja bikers. It shares DNA with other gloriously amateur 80s action like Raw Force (1982) and **Samurai Cop** (1991), but adds an earnest anti-drug message and inexplicable musical numbers. The film vanished after its initial release until Drafthouse Films rescued it in 2012, establishing it as a midnight movie sensation.

sections.content: The late 80s saw a fascinating wave of independent martial arts films trying to capitalize on the ninja craze sparked by **Enter the Ninja** (1981) and **American Ninja** (1985). These low-budget productions often featured real martial artists rather than trained actors, leading to fascinating combinations of authentic fighting technique and amateurish dramatic scenes. **Miami Connection** exemplifies this trend, with Y.K. Kim's legitimate Taekwondo skills on full display even as the plot careens wildly between motorcycle chases, beach training montages, and synthesizer-heavy musical performances.

What sets **Miami Connection** apart is its complete sincerity. Unlike later self-aware "bad" movies, there's no winking at the camera - Y.K. Kim genuinely wanted to make an anti-drug action epic that would inspire youth through martial arts and music. This earnestness elevates it above cynical exploitation films like **Ninja III: The Domination** (1984). The film's themes of friendship, perseverance, and staying drug-free may be handled with sledgehammer subtlety, but the conviction behind them is undeniable. SUBHEAD: The Legacy of Miami Connection

sections.content: The film's 2012 rediscovery sparked renewed interest in similar regional action films of the 1980s. Works like **Deadly Prey** (1987) and **Undefeatable** (1993) found new audiences through midnight screenings and boutique Blu-ray releases. This renaissance of appreciation for ambitious amateur filmmaking has influenced modern homages like **Kung Fury** (2015) and **WolfCop** (2014), though these newer films lack the pure conviction that makes **Miami Connection** so special.
